title: Why hallucination gates matter in clinical AI
subtitle: Hallucinations are not a language-model problem alone. They are a patient-safety problem.
excerpt: When a large language model invents a citation, the harm is reputational. When a clinical AI hallucinates a pulmonary embolism on a normal chest X-ray, the harm is a patient undergoing an unnecessary invasive procedure.
content:
Hallucination is a clinical safety problem

When a large language model invents a citation, the harm is reputational. When a clinical AI hallucinates a pulmonary embolism on a normal chest X-ray, the harm is a patient undergoing an unnecessary invasive procedure — or a radiologist losing trust in the entire category of AI assistance. Hallucination in clinical AI is not a technical curiosity; it is a patient-safety problem.

A hallucination occurs when the system produces an output that is confidently presented as a finding but is not supported by the input data. Unlike a random error, a hallucination is plausible — it looks like a real finding, uses the correct medical terminology, and is often accompanied by a high confidence score.
author: Dolapo Ariyo

evidence.claim: Pre-dispatch hallucination gate catches 96.3% of hallucinations (n=500)
Clinical AI hallucinations are a documented patient-safety concern
evidence.source: MHRA AI Airlock; NHS AI Lab
